{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''William Seymour Zwicker''' (born 1949) is an American [[mathematician]] and the William D. Williams Professor of Mathematics at [[Union College]] in [[Schenectady, New York]].<ref name="cv">[http://www.math.union.edu/people/faculty/cv/zwickerw.html Curriculum vitae], retrieved 2012-03-12.</ref>

Zwicker earned a bachelor's degree from [[Harvard University]] in 1971, and a Ph.D from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1976, under the supervision of Eugene M. Kleinberg. He joined the Union College faculty in 1975, was given his named chair in 2006, and retired in 2021.<ref name="cv"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=William Seymour Zwicker|id=62999}}</ref>

Zwicker has done research in [[set theory]] and [[social choice theory]]. He is credited with inventing the concept of a [[Finite Game#Supergame|supergame]] and the related [[Finite Game#Hypergame Paradox|hypergame paradox]].<ref name="Stanford">{{cite web |title=Self-Reference |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/self-reference/ |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |publisher=Stanford University |accessdate=2 March 2020 |date=Aug 31, 2017}}</ref> With Alan D. Taylor, he is the author of ''Simple Games: Desirability Relations, Trading, Pseudoweightings'' (Princeton University Press, 1999). Zwicker is also known for his work in [[fair division]], including for the [[Brams–Taylor–Zwicker procedure]] for envy-free cake cutting.
